sentences.text: The genus Echinodon contains only one known species, Echinodon becklesii.
Its name translates to "prickly tooth," referring to its unique dental anatomy, and the skull was estimated to be 62 mm long.
The premaxilla bore only three teeth without denticles, while the dentary contained eleven teeth, with the first two being specialized.
The lower jaw was deep for a basal ornithischian, reaching a height of 30% of its total length, and the animal was about 60 centimeters long.
Unlike other ornithischians, Echinodon possessed one or two canine-like teeth in each jaw.
This bipedal herbivore reached a length of approximately 60 centimeters.
Its premaxilla featured only three teeth that lacked denticles, a trait distinguishing it from most basal ornithischians.
Sir Richard Owen described the genus and the species Echinodon becklesii in 1861 after Samuel Beckles found multiple jaw bones on a cliff at Durdlestone Bay.
The specific name becklesii honors the collector who discovered the type specimen in the Purbeck Beds near Swanage, England.
In 1959, Justin Delair referred isolated dermal armour from the Purbeck Beds to Echinodon, but these fossils were later reassigned to solemydid turtles.
Butler et al. (2008) hypothesized that the enlarged canines of the clade were for an omnivorous diet, contrasting with Sereno's vegetation-cropping hypothesis.
Echinodon belongs to the family Heterodontosauridae, a classification established by Owen in 1861 and confirmed by Paul Sereno in 1991 based on divergent teeth.
Richard Thulborn placed Echinodon within the family Hypsilophodontidae in 1971, while Sereno was the first to reclassify it as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.
Echinodon lived during the earliest Cretaceous, specifically the Berriasian epoch, approximately 145 to 140 million years ago in southern England and possibly western France.

Sediments indicate the Purbeck Group was a lagoonal environment similar to the modern Mediterranean that became wetter over time, with a time range from the Kimmeridgian to the Berriasian, between 152.21 and 137.05 million years ago.

Echinodon was originally considered a herbivorous lizard but was quickly revised to be an intermediate ornithischian. It was once referred to the clade Stegosauria based on dental anatomy and incorrectly attributed armor that was later identified as belonging to a turtle. There is currently no evidence linking Echinodon to any specific bed in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Group. The presence of an arched diastema in Echinodon is a topic of disagreement among paleontologists. Galton considered Echinodon a fabrosaurid because its teeth lacked flat wear facets, despite similarities to Heterodontosauridae. Echinodon has occasionally been considered a basal thyreophore, mainly due to the erroneous association of osteoderms from a turtle member.
